title: Kafka: messages, keys and partitions
seriesDescription: A Kafka deep dive for system design interviews: why Kafka exists, terminology, messages and keys, offsets and replication, when to use it, scalability, hot partitions, fault tolerance, retries, performance and retention.
description: What is inside a message, how the key chooses the partition and then the broker, and why the log is append-only.
source: Study notes: Kafka deep dive for system design interviews

questions.prompt: Select all four fields of a Kafka message (record).

options.text: Value: the payload.
options.why: Yes: the data you send.

options.text: Key: decides which partition it goes to.
options.why: Yes: used for partitioning.

options.text: Timestamp: when it was created or ingested.
options.why: Yes; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Headers: key-value metadata like HTTP headers.
options.why: Yes; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: All four are technically optional; value is what you say, key is where it goes.

questions.prompt: What does a message key do?

options.text: Kafka hashes it to pick the partition, so the same key always lands on the same partition.
options.why: Right: same key, same partition, same order.

options.text: It encrypts the message value without any extra configuration.
options.why: Keys do not encrypt; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It chooses which consumer reads the message directly.
options.why: The consumer is chosen by the group assignment.

options.text: It sets how long the message is retained in a typical production setup.
options.why: Retention is a topic setting.

questions.explanation: Choosing the key is critical for ordering.

questions.prompt: What happens when a message has no key?

options.text: Kafka spreads messages across partitions with a default strategy, giving balance but no ordering.
options.why: Right: modern clients use a sticky partitioner.

options.text: The message is rejected by the broker for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Keys are optional; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: All keyless messages go to partition 0 under normal operating conditions.
options.why: They are spread out; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The message is stored on every partition as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: It goes to one partition.

questions.explanation: With a key you get ordering but risk imbalance; without one you get balance but lose ordering.

questions.prompt: Where does ordering inside a partition come from?

options.text: From offsets, not from timestamps.
options.why: Right: offsets are sequential per partition.

options.text: From the timestamp field, which is always unique.
options.why: Timestamps can collide and are not the order.

options.text: From the message value contents.
options.why: Kafka does not read the value.

options.text: From the producer's clock only.
options.why: Offsets decide order; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Offsets are assigned in append order.

questions.prompt: After hashing the key to a partition, how does the producer find the broker?

options.text: Cluster metadata kept by the controller maps each partition to its broker, and the producer sends straight there.
options.why: Right: key picks the partition, metadata picks the broker.

options.text: It broadcasts the message to every broker in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: It talks to one broker directly.

options.text: It asks a load balancer in front of Kafka.
options.why: Kafka clients talk to brokers directly.

options.text: It guesses and retries until a broker accepts for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: The mapping is known; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: The producer talks directly to the partition's leader broker.

questions.prompt: Why is Kafka's append-only log fast?

options.text: New messages are written only at the end, which keeps disk seeks to a minimum.
options.why: Right: seek time is a major storage bottleneck.

options.text: It keeps every message in RAM only.
options.why: It writes to disk; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It skips writing messages that nobody will read in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Everything is appended.

options.text: It compresses all history into one record under normal operating conditions.
options.why: History stays as separate messages.

questions.explanation: Never editing old data makes Kafka fast, safe and easy to scale.

questions.prompt: What does immutability of written messages simplify?

options.text: Replication and recovery, and it avoids the consistency problems of editable data.
options.why: Right: copies never diverge on edits.

options.text: Only the colour of the logs.
options.why: Not a technical benefit.

options.text: The ability to update a message in place as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: That is exactly what it prevents.

options.text: Deleting messages immediately on read without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: Messages leave by retention or compaction.

questions.explanation: Messages leave only through retention or log compaction.
